\chapter{See You Tomorrow}
\label{ch:la-see-you-tomorrow}
\hlchaptermodality{25}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say in Latin that I will see someone tomorrow, and say which piece of it Romance mostly abandoned.}

Say crās tē vidēbō on the same pattern, and say honestly that this combination is not itself a surviving quotation.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[crās tē vidēbō]{crās tē vidēbō — the same pattern, honestly not the same citation}

\label{lesson:LA-C25-cras-te-videbo}



\begin{quote}
Last lesson's phrase was a direct quote from Cicero. This one uses the exact same grammatical machinery — but be honest: it isn't itself pulled from a surviving letter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: crās tē vidēbō — built from known-good pieces}
\textbf{Crās tē vidēbō} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I'll see you tomorrow}\textquotedblright{} — swaps \textbf{crās} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{tomorrow}\textquotedblright{}) in for \emph{propediem} (\textquotedblleft{}soon\textquotedblright{}) from the last lesson, keeping the same \textbf{vidēbō} (\textquotedblleft{}I will see\textquotedblright{}) you already learned. Both pieces are genuinely classical: \emph{crās} is a real, common Latin adverb, and \emph{vidēbō} is the same attested future-tense verb as before. But be careful: unlike \emph{propediem tē vidēbō}, this \textbf{specific combination} isn't itself quoted in any surviving Roman letter — it's a well-formed construction built by analogy, not a direct citation.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Crās} traces back to \textbf{Proto-Italic} \emph{\textbf{*krās}} — but past that point, its ultimate origin is genuinely \textbf{uncertain}, with scholars proposing several different, competing Proto-Indo-European sources. Some things in etymology just don't resolve cleanly, even for a word this ordinary.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{culture}
Here's the real teaching point: \textbf{crās} didn't survive as the everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} in most of its major daughter languages. \textbf{French}'s \emph{demain}, \textbf{Italian}'s \emph{domani}, and \textbf{Catalan}'s \emph{demà} all rebuilt \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{} from \textbf{dē māne} (\textquotedblleft{}\textbf{in the morning}\textquotedblright{}) instead — the same morning-based logic reappearing three separate times. \textbf{Sardinian} and \textbf{Sicilian} are the main holdouts that kept \emph{crās} itself as an everyday word. Spanish, too, moved away from it, building its own \emph{mañana} on \textbf{māne} (\textquotedblleft{}morning\textquotedblright{}) rather than keeping \emph{crās}. A genuinely ordinary Latin word, abandoned by most of the family — echoing, if less completely, the same shape of story as \emph{flāvus} from the colors lesson (which survives nowhere as an everyday word, only in names like \emph{Flāvius}).
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}crās tē vidēbō\textquotedblright{} — \textquotedblleft{}I'll see you tomorrow\textquotedblright{}
  \item the honest caveat — same pattern as propediem tē vidēbō, but not itself a direct quotation
  \item the Romance twist — nearly everyone replaced crās with a morning-based word instead
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Is \textbf{crās tē vidēbō} itself quoted in a surviving Cicero letter, the way \emph{propediem tē vidēbō} was? (\textbf{No} — same grammatical pattern, built from two genuinely classical pieces, but not itself a direct citation.) Which Romance language kept \textbf{crās} as its everyday word for \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Sardinian and Sicilian} — most of the rest rebuilt it from \emph{dē māne}, \textquotedblleft{}in the morning,\textquotedblright{} instead.)
\end{tcolorbox}
